substitutions.technique: Sear in a dry-ish pan first; seitan browns faster than chicken and needs no cooking-through time.
substitutions.flavor_note: Season the poaching liquid, not just the surface — seitan takes salt the way chicken does not.
substitutions.why: Closest match on chew and protein density of anything in the table.

substitutions.technique: Press 20 minutes, then treat exactly as you would the chicken.
substitutions.flavor_note: A spoon of miso in the marinade replaces the savoury backbone chicken brings on its own.
substitutions.why: Gentler in flavour than seitan and easier to find.

substitutions.technique: Thighs forgive overcooking; so does tofu, once pressed. Same pan, same time.
substitutions.flavor_note: Thighs bring fat. Add a teaspoon of oil per portion so the dish does not read thin.
substitutions.why: Matches the fattier, more forgiving character of thigh meat.

substitutions.technique: Tear into strips rather than slicing — torn edges catch colour like skin does.
substitutions.flavor_note: Brown them hard. Undercooked mushrooms are the main reason a swap like this disappoints.
substitutions.why: The torn-strip texture is the nearest thing to shredded thigh.

substitutions.technique: Drop straight in where the beef went; it needs about a third less time to brown.
substitutions.flavor_note: Brown it harder than feels necessary — that crust is most of what beef was doing.
substitutions.why: One-for-one on mass, protein and browning behaviour.

substitutions.technique: Cook the lentils first, then add with the aromatics; they will not brown, so build colour on the onions.
substitutions.flavor_note: A spoonful of tomato paste and a splash of soy sauce carry the savoury weight beef was carrying.
substitutions.why: Much cheaper than plant mince and higher in fibre.

substitutions.technique: Chop fine and dry-fry until they squeak and the water is gone. Then oil.
substitutions.flavor_note: Mushrooms are the umami substitute; do not rinse the browned bits from the pan.
substitutions.why: Lowest-calorie route, and the one that tastes least like a substitute.

substitutions.technique: Cut into chunks and sear before braising. Cut the braise to 30 minutes — there is no collagen to break down.
substitutions.flavor_note: Keep the wine, the bay and the long-cooked aromatics; those were doing more than the beef was.
substitutions.why: Holds up to braising liquid without falling apart.

substitutions.technique: Rinse well, squeeze dry, then sear. It shreds on its own once it hits the liquid.
substitutions.flavor_note: Jackfruit is nearly flavourless and slightly sweet — go heavier on salt and acid than the recipe says.
substitutions.why: The shredded texture of slow-cooked chuck, in a fraction of the time.

substitutions.technique: Score the caps, marinate 15 minutes, then grill hard on both sides. Do not crowd the pan.
substitutions.flavor_note: Finish with flaky salt and a knob of butter or oil the way you would rest a steak.
substitutions.why: A whole cap eats like a steak: one piece, knife and fork.

substitutions.technique: Slice thin against the grain and sear fast and hot.
substitutions.flavor_note: A splash of soy and a little sugar in the pan gives you the crust that dry heat alone will not.
substitutions.why: Best protein match when the steak is being sliced into something.

substitutions.technique: Rinse, dry, sear, then simmer in the sauce for 25 minutes instead of hours.
substitutions.flavor_note: Pulled pork is mostly its sauce. Keep it, and add smoked paprika for the smoke the meat was carrying.
substitutions.why: Shreds like pulled pork with none of the cooking time.

substitutions.technique: Cube and brown, then braise 20 minutes.
substitutions.flavor_note: Add a little liquid smoke or smoked paprika — pork brings smoke that gluten does not.
substitutions.why: Keeps the protein where jackfruit would drop it.

substitutions.technique: Sear in chunks, then braise briefly.
substitutions.flavor_note: Lamb is carried by cumin, cinnamon and mint more than by the meat. Lean harder on all three.
substitutions.why: Sturdy enough for a long-cooked, heavily spiced dish.

substitutions.technique: Same pan, same time, slightly less oil.
substitutions.flavor_note: Turkey is mild, so the seasoning was already doing the work — change nothing else.
substitutions.why: The most direct swap in the table.

substitutions.technique: Slice thin, marinate 10 minutes, then fry in a little oil until the edges go dark.
substitutions.flavor_note: Soy sauce, maple syrup, smoked paprika and a drop of liquid smoke. All four, or it will not read as bacon.
substitutions.why: Bacon is smoke, salt, sugar and fat — every one of those can be added back.

substitutions.technique: Slice, toss in oil and salt, roast at 200°C until crisp at the edges.
substitutions.flavor_note: Same marinade as tempeh. Shiitake crisps better and brings its own savouriness.
substitutions.why: For dishes where bacon is a crunchy garnish rather than a component.

substitutions.technique: Brown gently; plant sausage splits if the pan is too hot.
substitutions.flavor_note: If the recipe leans on fennel or sage, add a pinch — most plant sausages are seasoned mildly.
substitutions.why: Direct swap, same shape, same cooking method.

substitutions.technique: Crumble in and fry hard so it catches.
substitutions.flavor_note: Smoked paprika and a little garlic and vinegar. Chorizo is a spice blend more than it is pork.
substitutions.why: Chorizo’s identity is almost entirely its paprika and fat, both of which transfer.

substitutions.technique: Cube and pan-fry, or roast with the glaze the recipe already calls for.
substitutions.flavor_note: A little maple and mustard puts back the sweet-salt cure.
substitutions.why: Firm enough to dice into a dish the way ham is used.

substitutions.technique: Slice into coins and crisp under the grill before adding, or it will steam.
substitutions.flavor_note: Fennel seed, chili flakes and paprika get you most of the way to pepperoni.
substitutions.why: The crisped-coin texture matters more than the meat.

substitutions.technique: Roast in thin slices until brittle, then crumble over at the end.
substitutions.flavor_note: Prosciutto is salt and umami in a very thin layer. Salt the mushrooms well.
substitutions.why: Both are used as a salty, crisp finishing note.

substitutions.technique: Press, then marinate at least 30 minutes so it takes colour. Roast or sear skin-side logic does not apply.
substitutions.flavor_note: Salmon brings oil. Do not skimp on the oil in the marinade, and finish with lemon.
substitutions.why: Takes a marinade deeply and holds together as a fillet-sized piece.

substitutions.technique: Slice the stems into coins and score a cross-hatch; they curl like shrimp when they hit heat.
substitutions.flavor_note: Cook fast and hot. Shrimp is a texture more than a flavour, and the texture comes from speed.
substitutions.why: The scored-coin trick is a genuinely close texture match.

substitutions.technique: Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole.
substitutions.flavor_note: Lemon, capers and a little seaweed or celery salt supply the brine that made it taste of the sea.
substitutions.why: Flaky when mashed and close on protein.

substitutions.technique: Press hard, cut into fillet-shaped pieces, dredge and pan-fry.
substitutions.flavor_note: White fish is delicate and salty. Keep it simple; lemon and salt do most of it.
substitutions.why: Mild enough not to fight the rest of the dish.

substitutions.technique: Melt into the oil at the same point the anchovies would have dissolved.
substitutions.flavor_note: Miso is saltier and sweeter. Start with less, taste, and add lemon at the end.
substitutions.why: Anchovy is a salt-and-umami delivery system; miso is the same thing without the fish.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap by volume.
substitutions.flavor_note: Add a squeeze of lime and a pinch of sugar; fish sauce is funkier and rounder than soy.
substitutions.why: Nearest common-cupboard match on salt and umami.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap.
substitutions.why: Standard worcestershire contains anchovy; the vegan version is otherwise identical.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap.
substitutions.flavor_note: Vegetable stock is thinner. A teaspoon of miso or soy per cup puts the body back.
substitutions.why: The one swap most recipes will not even notice.

substitutions.technique: For scrambles and custards: blend until smooth, then cook low and slow.
substitutions.flavor_note: A pinch of turmeric for colour and black salt (kala namak) for the sulphur note, if you have it.
substitutions.why: Silken tofu sets the way egg does when heated gently.

substitutions.technique: As a binder: whisk with an equal weight of water and rest 5 minutes before using.
substitutions.why: Binds like egg in patties, fritters and batters without adding flavour.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap. Soy curdles in very acidic batters; add acid last.
substitutions.why: Closest on protein and behaviour under heat of the common milks.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap, but it will not whip the same way. It will reduce and enrich the same way.
substitutions.flavor_note: In savoury dishes, coconut reads sweet. A squeeze of lemon and extra salt pulls it back.
substitutions.why: Matches the fat content, which is what cream was there for.

substitutions.technique: Blend soaked cashews with water to a pourable cream; add at the same point.
substitutions.why: Neutral where coconut is not, so it disappears into savoury sauces.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap for frying and finishing. In pastry, keep it cold the same way.
substitutions.why: Matched on fat, so the technique does not change.

substitutions.technique: Use less by weight; oil is pure fat where butter is about 80%.
substitutions.why: Better than vegan butter anywhere the dish is already Mediterranean.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap.
substitutions.why: Purpose-made for this and closest on salt.

substitutions.technique: Use about half the weight; it is far more intense.
substitutions.flavor_note: Add a pinch of salt with it — parmesan was bringing a lot of that.
substitutions.why: Cheaper and shelf-stable, with the same savoury hit.

substitutions.technique: Melts more reluctantly. Grate finer and cover the pan.
substitutions.why: Direct swap where cheddar is melted rather than tasted on its own.

substitutions.technique: Same. Give it a couple of extra minutes under the grill.
substitutions.why: Bred for stretch, which is the whole point of mozzarella.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap, though it is looser. Strain it if the dish needs thickness.
substitutions.flavor_note: Lemon juice puts back the tang that dairy fermentation gave it.
substitutions.why: Same role: cooling, acidic, spoonable.

substitutions.technique: Blend with lemon juice and salt to taste before using.
substitutions.flavor_note: Sour cream is sour. Cashew cream is not, until you make it so — do not skip the lemon.
substitutions.why: Matches the richness sour cream was providing.

substitutions.technique: Cube and marinate for an hour in oil, lemon, salt and oregano.
substitutions.flavor_note: Feta is brine. The marinade is not optional here; unmarinated tofu is just tofu.
substitutions.why: Takes on brine readily and crumbles the same way.

substitutions.technique: Blend with lemon, salt and a little olive oil until it is grainy, not smooth.
substitutions.why: Close on texture once blended, and far cheaper than cashew ricotta.

substitutions.technique: Blend thick, with lemon and salt.
substitutions.why: Same richness and spreadability.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap.
substitutions.why: Identical in use; the only difference is the egg.

substitutions.technique: Straight swap by volume.
substitutions.flavor_note: Maple is thinner and less floral. In a dressing, a little extra mustard rebalances it.
substitutions.why: Same sweetness and viscosity in most cooked applications.
